topics.title: Poledník a místní čas
topics.content: Polevník je čára, která spojuje oba zemské póly a má tvar polokružnice. Na každém polevníku nastává poledne ve stejný okamžik. V důsledku toho každý polevník má svůj vlastní místní čas.

topics.title: Časová pásma
topics.content: Pro zjednodušení je mít Zemi rozdělenou na časová pásma, která se navracejí po jedné hodině po 15 stupních. Na nulém polevníku (0°) je tzv. světový čas. Polevníky (0, 15, 30... až 180) procházejí vždy středem daného časového pásma. Časové pásmo je tedy vždy rozšířeno o 7,5° na východ od daného polevníku a 7,5° na západ.

topics.title: Datová hranice
topics.content: Datová hranice probíhá zhruba po 180. polevníku, což je stanovená hranice, na které se mění datum. Při přechodu západně-východě (VP→ZP) získáváme jeden den navíc, zatímco při přechodu východně-západě (ZP→VP) tento den ztrácíme.

topics.title: Výpočet místního času
topics.content: Výpočet vychází z předpokladu, že jedna hodina odpovídá 15° zeměpisné délky. Jeden stupeň (čepový) odpovídá za 4 minuty času. Teprve směrem na východ se čas přičítá, resp. na západ se odečítá.

topics.title: Definition and Position in Nature
topics.content: Viruses stand at the border between living and non‑living matter. They are considered the most primitive form of life but do not fulfill all basic properties of living organisms.

topics.title: Metabolism and Reproduction
topics.content: Viruses lack metabolism and cannot reproduce on their own. They become metabolically active only as intracellular parasites, obtaining the necessary machinery from the host cell.

topics.title: Parasitism
topics.content: The virus‑host relationship is parasitic: advantageous for the virus, detrimental for the host. Viruses are sub‑cellular particles (non‑cellular) and therefore are sometimes called sub‑cellular life forms.

topics.title: Virion Components
topics.content: A virion consists of a protein capsid that protects the genetic material (RNA or DNA). Some viruses contain only RNA and lack DNA entirely. The basic genetic unit is a gene (simple program).

topics.title: Capsid and Tail (Bičík)
topics.content: The capsid is a protein shell that can keep a virus viable on surfaces for up to 17 hours outside a host. Some viruses possess a tail (bičík) that may inject the genome into the host cell; the tail is optional.

topics.title: Envelope (Membrane)
topics.content: Certain viruses acquire a lipid envelope (membrane) during budding from the host cell, which can aid in entry and immune evasion.

topics.title: Lytic (Lyse) Cycle
topics.content: 1. Attachment to a specific cellular receptor. 2. Entry – either tail injection of nucleic acid or endocytosis of the whole virion. 3. Uncoating and transport of viral DNA/RNA to the nucleus (DNA viruses) or ribosomes (RNA viruses). 4. Hijacking host transcription/translation to produce viral proteins and genomes. 5. Assembly of new virions. 6. Release by cell lysis or budding.

topics.title: RNA Virus Replication
topics.content: RNA viruses bypass the nuclear entry step. Their RNA is directly translated by ribosomes to produce viral proteins, including capsid proteins and new RNA genomes. Advantage: no need to breach the nuclear membrane.

topics.title: Retroviruses
topics.content: Retroviruses carry RNA genomes that are reverse‑transcribed into DNA by reverse transcriptase. The resulting DNA integrates into the host genome. Reverse transcription is error‑prone, giving retroviruses a high mutation rate (e.g., HIV).

topics.title: Lysogenic (Lyzogenic) Cycle
topics.content: Initial steps mirror the lytic cycle, but the viral genome integrates into the host chromosome and replicates passively with host cell division. Under certain triggers the prophage is induced, entering the lytic phase. Lysogeny can promote uncontrolled host cell division, sometimes leading to cancer (e.g., HPV → cervical cancer, papillomavirus → warts).

topics.chapter: Overview of Viral Diseases and Prevention
topics.title: Therapy and Vaccination
topics.content: Most viral infections are treated symptomatically; specific antivirals exist for only a few viruses. Vaccination (active immunization) is the most effective preventive measure. Passive immunization provides pre‑formed antibodies.

topics.chapter: Overview of Viral Diseases and Prevention
topics.title: General Epidemiology
topics.content: Many viral diseases are highly contagious, especially in children. Some viruses (e.g., measles) have extremely high transmission rates.

topics.title: Childhood Exanthematous Diseases
topics.content: Common childhood viral illnesses include varicella (chickenpox), measles, rubella, and mumps. Typical course: fever followed by characteristic rash. Vaccination has eliminated most cases of measles, rubella and mumps; varicella remains common but is vaccine‑preventable.

topics.title: Poliomyelitis (Dětská obrna)
topics.content: Eradicated in the Czech Republic. The virus attacks the spinal cord, potentially causing paralysis and death.

topics.title: Influenza
topics.content: Targets respiratory epithelium, causing high fever, mucus production, and cough. Can be fatal; historic pandemics such as the 1918 Spanish flu caused tens of millions of deaths. Seasonal flu is usually milder; other respiratory viruses (adenoviruses, rhinoviruses, coronaviruses) cause similar but less severe symptoms.

topics.title: Tropical Viral Diseases
topics.content: Ebola (hemorrhagic fever, high mortality, African outbreaks). Dengue, yellow fever, chikungunya and Zika are mosquito‑borne; dengue and Zika can cause severe complications, while yellow fever is vaccine‑preventable.

topics.title: Rabies (Vzteklina)
topics.content: Transmitted by bites of carnivores (dogs, bats). Long incubation period, fatal once symptoms appear. Post‑exposure prophylaxis with vaccine is essential.

topics.title: Shingles (Pásový opar)
topics.content: Reactivation of varicella‑zoster virus in sensory ganglia, producing painful vesicular rash along a dermatome. Can persist for life, especially in immunocompromised individuals.

topics.title: Hepatitis (A–F)
topics.content: Inflammation of the liver. Hepatitis A – fecal‑oral transmission, usually mild, vaccine available. Hepatitis B – blood/sexual transmission, chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis and cancer; vaccine available. Hepatitis C, D, E, F – various transmission routes (blood, sexual, drug use); chronic forms may cause liver cancer. Treatment varies; vaccines exist for A and B.

topics.title: Infectious Mononucleosis
topics.content: Caused by Epstein‑Barr virus; attacks immune system and liver. Often asymptomatic or presents with fever, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy.

topics.title: HIV/AIDS
topics.content: Human immunodeficiency virus destroys CD4⁺ T‑lymphocytes, leading to immune collapse. Transmission: blood, sexual contact, mother‑to‑child. Antiretroviral therapy controls viral replication but does not cure infection. High mutation rate; vaccine still unavailable.

topics.title: Viroids
topics.content: Simplest infectious agents; consist only of short circular RNA without a protein capsid. Cause diseases in plants (e.g., potato spindle tuber).

topics.title: Prions
topics.content: Misfolded proteins that can induce abnormal folding of normal proteins. Cause transmissible spongiform encephalopathies such as Creutzfeldt‑Jakob disease in humans and bovine spongiform encephalopathy in cattle. Long incubation (≈20 years).

topics.title: Cellular Structures
topics.content: Typical bacterial cell features a cell wall, fimbriae (surface appendages for adhesion), and ribosomes for protein synthesis.
